assumptions: Assumes the app is part of the regulated processing context and lacks adequate rights-management features.
uncertainty_note: Actual rights-handling capabilities of the app are not described.

title: Receiving detailed inferred insights in the app may violate data minimization
description: If the app does not strictly need detailed risk indicators, routine summaries, and trend flags, receiving them constitutes processing more personal data than necessary for the stated function.
assumptions: Assumes some or all returned insight detail is not essential for the app's purpose.
uncertainty_note: Whether the data is excessive depends on the app's precise functional requirements, which are not specified.

title: Displayed inferred condition indicators enable linkage of sessions and records to the same individual profile
description: The app shares trend data and inferred eating-disorder or diabetes risk indicators with the wearer. These derived health-related outputs are profile-like data that can link multiple observations, sessions, or records to the same individual within the app context.
assumptions: Assumes the dashboard is tied to a persistent app account or device profile rather than being fully ephemeral and anonymous.

title: Health-risk indicators in transit are identifying through revealing attributes
description: The data flow contains highly revealing attributes, namely inferred eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals. Even without an explicit name in the payload, such sensitive health inferences can contribute to identifying or singling out the wearer when observed in transit or combined with context such as device ownership.
assumptions: Assumes the flow may be observable at least to the device UI layer, local notifications, or communication metadata/context rather than being perfectly shielded from all observers.

title: Displayed risk indicators can become attributable evidence about the wearer
description: By presenting inferred condition indicators to the user, the app creates data that can later be used as evidence that this wearer was assessed as having elevated eating-disorder or diabetes risk. Such records or screenshots could undermine deniability regarding the existence of those inferences.
assumptions: Assumes the dashboard content may be stored, cached, screenshot, logged, or otherwise retained beyond the immediate display.

title: System response reveals the existence of sensitive inferred conditions
description: The very presence and content of the dashboard response can reveal that the system has generated eating-disorder or diabetes risk indicators for this user. Anyone able to observe the response on screen or through notifications may detect the existence of a sensitive condition-related assessment.
assumptions: Assumes some possibility of shoulder surfing, lock-screen exposure, screen mirroring, or similar observation of the response.

title: App may disclose highly sensitive inferred health data beyond what is necessary for dashboard functionality
description: The source process shares inferred eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals with the user. These are highly sensitive health-related inferences; if the dashboard could fulfill its purpose with less sensitive or less explicit feedback, this flow discloses a more sensitive data type than functionally necessary.
assumptions: Assumes the same user value could be achieved through less explicit wellness feedback or lower-sensitivity presentation.
uncertainty_note: Necessity depends on product requirements and clinical justification, which are not provided.

title: User may be unaware that sensitive condition inferences are being generated and shown
description: The dashboard displays trends and inferred condition indicators, but the flow description does not indicate that the wearer is informed how these inferences were produced, what data was used, or what the indicators mean. This creates a risk of unawareness about sensitive processing affecting the data subject.

title: User may lack ability to challenge or remove incorrect inferred condition indicators
description: Once the wearer receives inferred eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals, there may be no apparent mechanism in this interaction for rectifying, contesting, or erasing incorrect or outdated inferences. This limits intervenability over sensitive personal data presented to the user.
assumptions: Assumes the app does not separately provide an effective correction, contestation, or deletion mechanism for these inferences.
uncertainty_note: The flow alone does not show whether such controls exist elsewhere in the system.

title: Displaying inferred sensitive health-risk assessments may create lawfulness concerns
description: The app shares inferred eating-disorder or diabetes risk indicators with the wearer. Because these are sensitive health-related inferences and may resemble profiling or automated assessment, this processing may raise legal compliance issues if not supported by an appropriate lawful basis and safeguards.
assumptions: Assumes the inferred indicators qualify as sensitive personal data or sensitive inferences under the applicable regime.
uncertainty_note: Specific legal applicability depends on jurisdiction, lawful basis, and whether the indicators are purely informational or used for decisions.

title: Sharing full health and location dataset enables linkage via quasi-identifiers
description: The Health Analytics Service shares the full health and location dataset with the cloud provider. Combinations of health attributes, location data, and analytics outputs can act as quasi-identifiers, enabling records about the same individual to be linked across datasets or replicas.

title: Cloud-hosted analytics data and models can be used to profile and link individuals
description: Once received by the cloud hosting provider, the hosted analytics data, models, and full health and location dataset may support profiling that links multiple records, behaviors, or inferred traits to the same individual.

title: Full health and location dataset is identifiable through quasi-identifiers
description: By transmitting the full health and location dataset, the source exposes combinations of attributes that can uniquely identify or single out data subjects even if direct identifiers are absent.

title: Transfer metadata may reveal identified information
description: The data flow to a third-party cloud provider may include file, transport, or object metadata that reveals identified information about data subjects, tenants, or the sending service during transmission.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not explicitly mention metadata contents; this threat is plausible for hosted dataset transfers but not certain from the provided context alone.

title: Received health and location data contains revealing attributes supporting identification
description: At the cloud provider, the received dataset contains highly revealing health and location attributes that can support identification of data subjects, especially when stored together with analytics artifacts and replicas.

title: Hosted dataset can serve as attributable evidence about individuals
description: By sending the full health and location dataset for hosting and replication, the source creates records that may later be used to attribute conditions, movements, or behaviors to specific individuals, undermining deniability.

title: Transfer metadata may create attributable evidence
description: Transmission and hosting transfers commonly generate metadata such as timestamps, object names, routing, or account context that can be used as evidence linking data or actions to particular individuals or entities.
uncertainty_note: The exact metadata generated on this flow is not specified, so applicability depends on implementation details.

title: Cloud-hosted transfer makes sensitive communications observable
description: Sending analytics data, models, and the full health and location dataset to an external cloud provider creates an observable communication event whose existence may reveal that sensitive health-related processing and storage are taking place.

title: Source discloses sensitive dataset to an additional predetermined external party
description: The Health Analytics Service shares analytics data, models, and the full health and location dataset with a third-party cloud hosting provider. This exposes sensitive personal data to an additional fixed external party, which may exceed what is strictly necessary depending on architecture choices.

title: Full health and location dataset may be more sensitive than necessary to host
description: The source sends the full health and location dataset, which includes highly sensitive health and precise location information. Providing the full dataset to the cloud provider may disclose more sensitive data types than are functionally required for hosting analytics outputs.
uncertainty_note: The description says the full dataset is hosted, but it does not confirm whether a reduced or transformed dataset would have sufficed.

title: Replication at the cloud provider propagates personal data beyond the immediate hosting need
description: The destination hosts and replicates the analytics data and full health and location dataset. Replication increases propagation and accessibility of sensitive personal data across storage locations or internal services, potentially beyond what is strictly necessary.

title: Cloud hosting and replication may extend retention of sensitive data
description: Hosting and replication at the cloud provider can result in copies of the full health and location dataset being retained in backups, replicas, or storage tiers longer than functionally needed.
uncertainty_note: The flow description mentions hosting and replication but does not specify retention periods; the threat is inferred from common cloud replication behavior.

title: Data subjects may be unaware their health and location data is hosted by a third-party cloud provider
description: By transferring the full health and location dataset to an external cloud hosting provider, the source may cause processing and storage by a third party that data subjects are not aware of.

title: Replication at the cloud provider can hinder erasure or rectification
description: Once the cloud provider receives and replicates the full health and location dataset, correcting or deleting personal data may become harder across replicas, backups, and distributed storage locations, reducing practical intervenability for data subjects.

title: Sharing the full dataset with the cloud provider may violate data minimization
description: Transferring the full health and location dataset, together with analytics data and models, to a third-party cloud provider may involve processing more personal data than necessary for the hosting purpose, creating GDPR data minimization concerns.

title: Cloud replication may conflict with storage limitation obligations
description: Replication and hosted storage at the cloud provider can lead to personal data being kept in multiple copies or backups longer than necessary, creating risk of violating storage limitation requirements.
uncertainty_note: Retention settings and contractual controls are not described, so this is a plausible compliance risk rather than a confirmed violation.

title: Third-party hosting of sensitive health and location data may raise lawfulness concerns
description: Sending the full health and location dataset to an external cloud provider for hosting and replication may require a clear lawful basis and appropriate safeguards due to the sensitivity of the data and involvement of a third party.
uncertainty_note: The applicable lawful basis, processor arrangements, and safeguards are not provided, so this is a risk indicator rather than a confirmed noncompliance finding.
